0155.event: At Pinnacle Point in South Africa, about one hundred sixty-four thousand years ago, the tide went out, and the people went down to the rocks with baskets woven from river grass. Mussels, limpets, periwinkles: pried from the stone, carried up the cliff, roasted on the coals till the shells popped open. The first seafood feast in the record, and the smell of it is still there in the mind's eye: salt and smoke and laughter, children burning their fingers, an old man sucking a shell clean. They did not know they were making history. They were just hungry, and the sea was generous, and supper was good.
0155.announce: Supper's ready, in a seaside song: The Shellfish Supper.
0155.title: The Shellfish Supper
0155.piece:
The tide went out at Pinnacle Point.
The people gathered, joint by joint,
the mussels from the rocks below.
The baskets filled. The coals would glow.
One hundred sixty-four thousand years.
The shells popped open. Laughter. Cheers.
Salt and smoke on the evening air.
The children burned their fingers there.
An old man sucked a shell clean.
The best supper ever seen.
They didn't know they'd made the past.
They only knew the feast would last
in memory. The sea was kind.
The first seafood feast, we find,
was supper, plain and simply good.
We eat the same, as eaters should.

0156.event: At Herto in Ethiopia, about one hundred sixty thousand years ago, skulls were polished and cut-marked and handled with care long after death. Not butchery, but reverence, of a kind we have no name for anymore. Watch the hands do it in the mind's eye: slow, deliberate, defleshing with care and setting aside. They kept the heads of their dead the way you keep a letter from someone gone. What did they believe? The rite is sealed. But tenderness is recognizable across any distance, even a hundred sixty thousand years, and those polished skulls seem to have been loved. That much seems likely.
0156.announce: Polished with love, in a rite verse: The Herto Skulls.
0156.title: The Herto Skulls
0156.piece:
At Herto, the skulls were kept with care,
polished, cut-marked, handled there
long after death had done its part.
This was not butchery. This was heart.
One hundred sixty thousand years.
The hands were slow. There were no fears,
only reverence, deep and true,
the way the living honor you
when you are gone. They kept the head
the way you keep the words once said
by someone loved. The rite is sealed.
But love is love, and love revealed
itself in polish, cut, and keep.
The dead seem loved. The love runs deep.

0157.event: Somewhere in Africa, about one hundred fifty thousand years ago, a man lived whose Y chromosome marches on in every living man today. Son to son to son, an unbroken thread, through ten thousand generations, through the founding of every nation, through every war and every peace. He never knew. He was one man among thousands, hunting, fathering sons, growing old, sweating in the same sun as all the rest. But the thread runs through him like a single red line through the whole tapestry. Every father is his heir, whether he knows it or not. The thread never broke.
0157.announce: Son to son, in a thread song: The Father of All.
0157.title: The Father of All
0157.piece:
Somewhere a man walked, long ago,
where the African winds still blow.
One hundred fifty thousand years.
He hunted. He laughed. He knew no fears
of being forgotten, for the thread
runs on, though he is dead.
Son to son, the Y goes on,
from dusk of man to breaking dawn.
Ten thousand generations deep,
the fathers keep what fathers keep.
He never knew. How could he tell?
He was one man, and all was well.
But every man alive today
carries his line. It lights the way.
The thread runs red. It never parts.
It runs through all our hearts.

0158.event: At Dar es-Soltan in Morocco, about one hundred forty thousand years ago, families sheltered in sea caves as the climate swung wild between green and dry. Green years when the rains came, lean years when the hills went brown. Sit with them through a dry season in the mind's eye: mothers stretching the last of the grain, children learning which roots would not kill them. The sea breathed below the cliffs, and the caves held the dark. They endured because they bent, because they knew the green would come back, as it always had. Patience was the whole of the strategy, and it worked.
0158.announce: Bend, don't break, in a shelter verse: The Caves by the Sea.
0158.title: The Caves by the Sea
0158.piece:
The caves face the Atlantic wide.
The families sheltered deep inside.
One hundred forty thousand years,
through the green times, through the fears
of the lean years. The climate swung.
The old songs were still sung.
Mothers stretched the grain out thin.
The children learned which roots would win
against hunger. The sea breathed low.
The caves held dark. The winds would blow.
They bent. They did not break. They knew
the green would come, as green will do.
Patience was the strategy, and true:
it worked for them. It works for you.

0159.event: In Tabun Cave in Israel, about one hundred thirty thousand years ago, a Neanderthal was laid to rest in the earth with intention. Not dropped, not left, but placed: laid down, it seems on purpose, in a dug hollow. The dead begin to be treated as people still, and grief may have dug one of its first deliberate graves. Stand at the grave's edge in the mind's eye, and it is there: perhaps the first time someone put something precious in a hole on purpose, because it mattered. He was one of the others, the cold people, and they buried him like one of their own. Grief is older than our name for it.
0159.announce: Laid to rest, in a grief verse: The Tabun Burial.
0159.title: The Tabun Burial
0159.piece:
In Tabun Cave, they laid him down,
a Neanderthal, of some renown
among his own. Not dropped. Not tossed.
But placed, as one who counted, lost
to the living, kept by the dead.
They dug the hollow for his head,
his limbs, his rest. One hundred thirty
thousand years. The earth was hearty
enough to hold him. Grief dug deep
that day, and laid him down to sleep
on purpose. Perhaps the first deliberate grave.
We bury still. We still are brave
enough to say: you mattered. Rest.
The dead were people. That is best.

0160.event: At Skhul in Israel, about one hundred twenty thousand years ago, modern humans buried their dead with wild-boar jaws clasped in their hands: grave goods for the road ahead, among the first graves of our kind. Watch them dig in the cave floor in the mind's eye, arrange the limbs with care, and see a mother press a jawbone into her son's curled fingers. They may have believed that something of us goes on, that the dead need provisions. Hope, laid in the earth with the body. The oldest luggage for the longest journey, packed with love.
0160.announce: Provisions for the longest journey, a poem: The Skhul Dead.
0160.title: The Skhul Dead
0160.piece:
At Skhul they buried their own dead,
and in their hands, the boar jaws laid.
One hundred twenty thousand years.
A mother's love, a mother's fears,
pressed in the jawbone, curled and tight,
in her son's fingers, in the night
of the cave. Among the first graves,
our kind dug deep, as dug the waves
of time. They may have thought the dead would need
provisions. Hope was the seed
they planted with the body, deep.
The longest journey, laid to sleep
with luggage. Love goes down below.
The dead still travel. This we know.

0161.event: At Contrebandiers Cave in Morocco, about one hundred fifteen thousand years ago, pierced sea-snail shells became beads: tiny spirals from the tide line, strung into jewelry tens of thousands of years older than any painting. Watch a girl hold hers to the light in the mind's eye, turning it this way and that. This was not about warmth or food or survival at all. This was about being beautiful in a world that had never asked for beauty. The first necklace in history was a love letter to being alive, and we have been writing that letter ever since.
0161.announce: Beauty for its own sake, a song: The Necklace of the Sea.
0161.title: The Necklace of the Sea
0161.piece:
Pierced shells from the tide line's edge,
strung on a cord, a beaded pledge
of beauty. One hundred fifteen thousand years.
A girl holds hers. The light appears
through the spiral. She turns it so.
This is for beauty. This we know.
Not warmth, not food, not need, but grace.
The first necklace in the human race.
The sea gave shells. The hands gave art.
The love letter of the heart
to being alive. We wear it still,
the sea's small gift, against our will
to be plain. We choose to shine.
The necklace says: be beautiful. Be mine.

0162.event: At Katanda in the Congo, about one hundred ten thousand years ago, barbed harpoons carved from bone pulled giant catfish from the Semliki River. The deep water yielded to the first true fishing tools. Watch a fisherman wade in at dawn in the mind's eye, water to his thighs, spear raised, and the river gives up a monster that feeds his family for days. Bone against scale, hunger against the deep. The river always gives, but only to the ones who learn its tools. The harpoon was the key, and the river was the lock, and the fisherman turned it.
0162.announce: Bone against scale, in a river verse: The Bone Harpoons.
0162.title: The Bone Harpoons
0162.piece:
Katanda. The Semliki flows.
The barbed bone harpoon knows
the way to the giant catfish deep.
The fisherman will wade, will keep
his spear raised at the dawn's first light.
The river gives up, in the fight,
a monster for the family's days.
One hundred ten thousand years, the ways
of water. Bone against the scale.
Hunger will at last prevail.
The deep gives only to the skilled.
The harpoon strikes. The net is filled.
The river's key was carved from bone.
We fish the same. The skill's our own.

0163.event: About one hundred five thousand years ago, modern humans pressed out of Africa again, following the coasts as the ice loosened. Not the first to try, but the ones who stayed: family by family, fire by fire, along the shellfish beds and the easy water, into the Levant and beyond, carrying everything they owned on their backs and everything they were in their blood. The second wave. The one that never came home. Every one of us outside Africa is walking in their footprints still, and the coasts they followed are still the roads we travel.
0163.announce: The wave that never came home, a song: The Second Wave.
0163.title: The Second Wave
0163.piece:
Out of Africa, once again,
they walked through sun and rain.
One hundred five thousand years ago,
the second wave began to flow
along the coasts, the easy way,
fire by fire, day by day.
Not the first to try. But they stayed.
The footprints that they made
are ours. We walk them even now.
Every one of us knows how
it feels to leave and not return.
The wave taught us. We still learn.
They carried all they were, and went.
The world was wide. The wave was sent.
It never came home. It lives in you.
The second wave still carries through.

0164.event: At Blombos Cave in South Africa, about one hundred thousand years ago, red ochre was mixed with fat and charcoal in abalone shells: the first artist's studio, where paint was made. Someone sat in the lamplight, mixing red like a cook mixing stew, testing the color on a fingertip, planning a wall, a body, a story. Art had a kitchen before it had a gallery. The smell of it is still there in the mind's eye: sweet and earthy, fat and ochre, in the cool cave air. A hundred thousand years ago, someone decided the world needed color, and made it.
0164.announce: Red like a cook mixes stew, a verse: The Paint Workshop.
0164.title: The Paint Workshop
0164.piece:
Abalone shells for mixing bowls,
red ochre for the artist's goals.
One hundred thousand years ago,
the paint began to flow.
Fat and charcoal, stirred with care,
the sweet smell hanging in the air.
Someone sat in the lamplight's glow,
mixing red, as cooks all know
to mix. A fingertip to test.
The color had to be the best.
A wall, a body, a story planned.
The first studio in the land.
Art had a kitchen, small and true,
before the gallery ever grew.
We mix the paint. We make the hue.
The workshop's red still carries through.

0165.event: At Qafzeh in Israel, about one hundred thousand years ago, a child was buried holding deer antlers: thirteen years old, give or take, with the antlers laid in his arms like a bouquet of bone. Someone may have carried those antlers far, may have chosen them and placed them, so that the boy would hold something beautiful wherever he was going. Stand with the mourners in the cave mouth in the mind's eye. A hundred thousand years later, the weight of it is still there: the particular, unbearable weight of a parent burying a child, and refusing to let him go empty-handed. Grief made visible.
0165.announce: A bouquet of bone, in a mourning poem: The Boy with the Antlers.
0165.title: The Boy with the Antlers
0165.piece:
At Qafzeh, they buried a child,
thirteen years, gentle and mild.
Deer antlers in his arms, like flowers
of bone, for the dark hours.
Perhaps someone carried them from far.
Perhaps someone chose them, like a star
to guide him where he had to go.
A hundred thousand years ago,
a parent could not let him leave
with empty hands. We still grieve
the same way. The weight is true:
the unbearable, for me and you,
of burying the young, and yet
refusing to forget.
The antlers say: you were loved.
Grief made visible. Grief proved.

0166.event: At Qafzeh in Israel, about ninety-five thousand years ago, red ochre stains the burials. The dead go down painted: faces dusted, bodies reddened, as if the color could warm them on the road they were taking. Watch the mourners grind the stone in the mind's eye, mix the powder, anoint the still faces. Think of blood, of birth, of sunsets: all the red things that mean life. They painted the dead the color of the living. Perhaps they believed the color would carry over. Perhaps they just could not bear the gray. Either way, the dead go down painted, and love goes down with them.
0166.announce: The color of the living, a verse: The Qafzeh Ochre.
0166.title: The Qafzeh Ochre
0166.piece:
Red ochre on the still, cold face.
The dead go down with color, grace.
Ninety-five thousand years ago,
the mourners ground the red to show
their love. The faces dusted red,
the bodies painted for the dead
road ahead. Like blood, like birth,
like sunsets on the earth.
The color of the living, worn
by the dead, from dusk to morn.
Perhaps it warms. Perhaps it stays
as love, through all the days.
The gray was more than they could bear.
So red went down. Love's color. There.

0167.event: At Blombos in South Africa, about ninety thousand years ago, an ochre slab carries deliberate cross-hatching: no animal, no hunt, no story to read, just pattern for its own sake. Someone sat with a sharp stone and made geometry out of red rock, line crossing line crossing line, because the pattern pleased them. Run a finger along the grooves in the mind's eye, and there is the oldest itch in the world: to make a mark and mean it. The seed of writing, planted ninety thousand years early in ochre, waiting for rain. We have been drawing lines ever since.
0167.announce: Line crossing line, in a pattern poem: The Engraved Stone.
0167.title: The Engraved Stone
0167.piece:
An ochre slab, cross-hatched with care,
lines crossing lines, laid bare.
Ninety thousand years ago,
someone let the pattern flow.
No animal. No hunt. No tale.
Just the lines, beyond the veil
of meaning. Pattern for its own
sake, cut in red-brown stone.
The oldest itch: to make a mark
and mean it, in the dark.
The seed of writing, planted deep,
in ochre, for the years to keep.
Line on line, the pattern grows.
We draw the lines. The river flows
of ink, of thought, of all we say.
It started here. It starts today.

0168.event: High in the mountains of Teshik-Tash in Uzbekistan, about eighty-five thousand years ago, a Neanderthal child was buried ringed with ibex horns: a crown of the wild goat's pride around a small still head. Tenderness at the roof of the world, where the wind never stops and the winters kill the unready. Kneel in that thin cold air in the mind's eye, and look at the circle of horns. Whoever arranged these loved that child the way we love ours: fiercely, uselessly, forever. The mountains remember nothing. But the horns remember everything.
0168.announce: A crown of horns, in a mountain elegy: The Teshik-Tash Child.
0168.title: The Teshik-Tash Child
0168.piece:
High in the mountains, cold and steep,
a Neanderthal child lies asleep.
Ringed with ibex horns, a crown
of the wild goat, laid gently down.
Eighty-five thousand years ago,
where the high winds always blow.
Tenderness at the roof of the sky.
We loved our children. So did they. Why
would it be otherwise? The horns
were placed with love. The heart mourns
the small one, gone too soon, too fast.
The mountains' memory will not last.
But horns remember. Love remains.
The crown of horns still speaks, still pains
with beauty. Fiercely, uselessly,
forever. Love will always be.

0169.event: In Africa, about eighty-three thousand years ago, body lice split from head lice, and a tiny parasite testified to something enormous: someone may have been wearing sewn skins. Body lice live in clothing, so the split means the clothes existed. No needle survives, no thread, no hide. Only the louse. Picture her in the mind's eye: cold evening, a hide, a bone awl, sinew thread, stitching warmth around her children. The smallest witness in history testifies that we got dressed, and never really got undressed again. The first tailor is lost. The first clothes are proven by a louse.
0169.announce: The smallest witness, in a tailor's verse: The First Clothes.
0169.title: The First Clothes
0169.piece:
No needle left. No thread, no hide.
Only a louse to testify, so wide
the gap of time. Eighty-three thousand years.
The body louse confirms our fears
and hopes: we may have worn sewn skins back then.
Picture her, the first of women and men
who stitched: cold evening, bone awl, thread
of sinew, wrapping round the bed
of children. Warmth, sewn stitch by stitch.
The smallest witness. Life's first switch
from naked to the clothed, the kept.
We got dressed. We never slept
naked again. The louse still knows.
The first tailor's story grows
with every stitch we sew today.
We dress the same old way.

0170.event: At Taforalt in Morocco, about eighty thousand years ago, pierced shells stained red with ochre were strung into necklaces, bead by bead. Each one a small red sun to wear against the throat. Watch the stringing by firelight in the mind's eye: the careful hands, the choosing, this shell, not that one, the small vanities of the very old world. Eighty thousand years, and we still do it: still pick, still pierce, still wear what the sea gives us, still trying to be beautiful for each other. The necklace is the oldest unbroken fashion, and the sea is still the jeweler.
0170.announce: Small red suns, in a stringing song: The Taforalt Beads.
0170.title: The Taforalt Beads
0170.piece:
Pierced shells, stained red with ochre's glow,
strung bead by bead, row on row.
Eighty thousand years ago,
by the fire's light, soft and low,
the careful hands chose, shell by shell.
This one. Not that. They knew well
the small vanities of the heart.
Each bead a sun, each sun a part
of the necklace. Wear it true.
The sea gives still, for me and you.
We pick, we pierce, we wear, we shine.
The oldest fashion's yours and mine.
Small red suns against the throat.
The sea's the jeweler. Take note.

0171.event: At Sibudu Cave in South Africa, about seventy-seven thousand years ago, sleepers piled sedges and sweet-smelling leaves into the first mattresses. Armfuls of soft river grass, deep in the shelter's back, with the fragrant leaves on top to keep the insects away. Lie down on one in the mind's eye, and feel the give of it, the grassy smell, the small luxury of not sleeping on stone. Seventy-seven thousand years ago, someone decided that rest deserved comfort: that the body, after the hunt, after the cold, earned something soft. Every bed since is a descendant of that pile of grass.
0171.announce: Rest deserved comfort, in a sleepy verse: The First Bed.
0171.title: The First Bed
0171.piece:
Armfuls of sedge, piled deep,
where the ancient sleepers sleep.
Seventy-seven thousand years.
The sweet leaves calm the fears
of insects. Lie down. Feel the give,
the grassy smell. Learn to live
softly, after the hunt, the cold.
The body earns what the night will hold:
comfort. Someone decided true
that rest deserved its comfort too.
Not stone, but sedge. Not hard, but deep.
The first mattress. Time to sleep.
Every bed since, far and wide,
is that pile of grass, inside.
We sleep the same. The dream's the same.
Comfort was the first true aim.

0172.event: At Blombos in South Africa, about seventy-five thousand years ago, forty-one pierced and carefully notched shells became a bracelet. Count them with the maker in the mind's eye: one, two, three, the rhythm of the work, the choosing and the piercing, the small pride of a finished thing. A bracelet is a small claim, worn on the wrist where everyone can see: I was here, I made this, I am someone. The sea gave the shells. The hand gave the meaning. And meaning, it turns out, was the whole point. Seventy-five thousand years later, we are still making the same claim.
0172.announce: I was here, in a bracelet song: The Beads of Blombos.
0172.title: The Beads of Blombos
0172.piece:
Forty-one shells, pierced with care,
notched and strung, for the wrist to wear.
Seventy-five thousand years ago,
the maker let the meaning flow.
One, two, three, the rhythm true,
the choosing, piercing, all for you
to see. A bracelet's small claim:
I was here. I made this. I am. My name
in shells. The sea gave. The hand gave more:
the meaning. That's what bracelets are for.
We wear the same claim even now.
The wrist still speaks. We know how.
I was here. The shells still say.
We make our meaning, day by day.

0173.event: On Sumatra, about seventy-four thousand years ago, Mount Toba blew the top off the world. The sky went black at noon, and the ash fell for years: a volcanic winter that may have thinned humanity to a few thousand shivering souls. Walk through that darkness in the mind's eye. The sun was a rumor. The crops were a memory. Everything green turned gray and died. And yet, around a few stubborn fires, people held on: shared the last food, kept the children warm, told stories in the endless dusk. We came that close to never happening. Every human alive may descend from those who would not die in the dark.
0173.announce: When the sun was a rumor, a verse: The Sky Goes Dark.
0173.title: The Sky Goes Dark
0173.piece:
Toba blew the top off the sky.
The ash fell. The sun asked why,
and got no answer. Black at noon.
The world went dark, and none too soon
for comfort. Seventy-four thousand years.
A few thousand souls, through fears,
held on around the stubborn fires.
They shared the food. They sang the choirs
of stories in the endless dusk.
The green world turned to gray dust.
And yet they would not die. They stayed.
The children warm. The debts all paid
in courage. We may be their seed.
We are the ones who wouldn't concede.
The sky went dark. We kept the light.
We are the children of that night.

0174.event: In South Africa, about seventy-two thousand years ago, leaf-shaped spearheads thinned to perfection flew from Still Bay workshops along the southern coast. Stone leaves, sharp as intent, balanced like a thought. Watch a knapper work one down in the mind's eye, flake by careful flake. In the shadow of Toba's ash, craft may have leapt forward. Beauty became a weapon, and the weapon became beautiful. The world had tried to end, and the workshops answered with better blades. Necessity is the mother of the edge, and the Still Bay knappers were her finest children.
0174.announce: Sharp as intent, in a knapper's song: The Still Bay Points.
0174.title: The Still Bay Points
0174.piece:
Leaf-shaped, thinned to perfection's edge,
the Still Bay points make their pledge:
sharp as intent, balanced true,
the finest stone the knappers knew.
Seventy-two thousand years ago,
in Toba's shadow, the workshops glow
with craft. Flake by careful flake,
the stone leaves that the hunters take.
Beauty became the weapon's art.
The weapon played the beauty's part.
The world had tried to end, you see.
The answer: craft. And keep it free,
and keep it keen. The points still fly.
We make them still. You wonder why?
Because the best is what we do.
The Still Bay points fly true.
